nodes.title: Requirements, capacity, and architecture decomposition
nodes.coverageFocus: Problem framing, scope, workload estimates, SLOs, critical flows, and high-level decomposition
nodes.boundary: Separate product requirements and quality targets from implementation choices; estimates must drive decisions rather than decorate the answer.

nodes.title: API contracts, service boundaries, and request flows
nodes.coverageFocus: External and internal contracts, communication style, idempotency, deadlines, versioning, quotas, and service boundaries
nodes.boundary: Distinguish protocol mechanics from domain boundaries; a fashionable API style is not automatically the correct contract.

nodes.title: Data models, storage selection, indexing, and transactions
nodes.coverageFocus: Access-pattern-first modeling, engine selection, indexes, invariants, transactions, lifecycle, migrations, and search
nodes.boundary: Choose storage from access patterns and invariants, not from data labels alone; separate source-of-truth storage from derived indexes and caches.

nodes.title: Caching, read scaling, search, and content delivery
nodes.coverageFocus: Cache placement, invalidation, stale data, hot keys, read replicas, materialized views, CDN, and search serving
nodes.boundary: Caching is a consistency decision, not a universal speed switch; distinguish authoritative data, derived views, and disposable acceleration layers.

nodes.title: Partitioning, replication, consistency, and coordination
nodes.coverageFocus: Sharding, replication, consistency guarantees, consensus, coordination, distributed atomicity, clocks, and cross-region locality
nodes.boundary: Do not conflate availability, durability, consistency, and ordering; every guarantee must be tied to a concrete read/write path and failure model.

nodes.title: Messaging, streaming, jobs, workflows, and backpressure
nodes.coverageFocus: Queues, pub/sub, logs, delivery semantics, ordering, retries, DLQs, stream processing, workflows, and durable jobs
nodes.boundary: Messaging products are not interchangeable; distinguish transient commands, durable work, event notification, replayable history, and workflow state.

nodes.title: Reliability, fault isolation, resilience, and disaster recovery
nodes.coverageFocus: Failure modes, fault domains, resilience patterns, overload protection, graceful degradation, backups, failover, RPO, and RTO
nodes.boundary: Redundancy does not automatically provide recoverability; separate fault tolerance, backup, disaster recovery, graceful degradation, and overload behavior.

nodes.title: Security, identity, tenancy, privacy, and abuse controls
nodes.coverageFocus: Authentication, authorization, service identity, secrets, tenant isolation, encryption, abuse prevention, privacy, and threat modeling
nodes.boundary: Authentication is not authorization, encryption is not isolation, and client-side controls are not enforcement; define explicit trust boundaries.

nodes.title: Observability, operability, deployments, and evolution
nodes.coverageFocus: Telemetry, SLOs, alerting, health, rollout, rollback, compatibility, incidents, toil, and operational ownership
nodes.boundary: Telemetry without decisions is noise; distinguish detection, diagnosis, safe rollout, recovery, and long-term operability.

nodes.title: Performance, capacity, cost, and architecture trade-offs
nodes.coverageFocus: Critical paths, saturation, scaling, queueing, load testing, unit economics, managed-vs-built choices, and staged evolution
nodes.boundary: Performance and cost decisions must preserve correctness and reliability; do not optimize a component without considering the end-to-end critical path.

competencies.statement: Clarify actors, core use cases, system boundary, and explicit out-of-scope behavior.
Derive measurable latency, availability, durability, consistency, privacy, and operability requirements.
Estimate traffic, concurrency, storage, growth, and peak-to-average workload shape at useful order-of-magnitude precision.
Decompose the system into responsibilities, identify critical flows and bottlenecks, and iterate through trade-offs clearly.
Design resource, command, event, and query contracts with clear semantics and ownership.
Choose synchronous, asynchronous, RPC, streaming, or event communication from latency, coupling, and delivery requirements.
Assign deadlines, timeouts, cancellation, retries, idempotency, rate limits, and overload behavior to the correct boundary.
Evolve APIs and service boundaries without silently breaking callers, stored data, or rolling deployments.
Derive logical and physical data models from access patterns, ownership, invariants, and lifecycle.
Select storage, indexes, search, and derived projections from query, scale, consistency, and operational requirements.
Place transaction boundaries and concurrency controls so business invariants remain valid under concurrent access.
Plan retention, archival, deletion, schema migration, and online data evolution.
Choose cache placement and read/write strategy from ownership, freshness, cost, and failure requirements.
Use replicas, materialized views, precomputation, and derived stores without confusing them with the source of truth.
Design CDN, edge, and search-serving paths with explicit personalization, freshness, and fallback boundaries.
Prevent hot keys, stampedes, thundering herds, and stale-data amplification.
Choose partition keys, rebalancing strategies, and hotspot mitigations from workload distribution.
Choose replication topology and consistency guarantees from read/write paths and failure requirements.
Reason about consensus, leader election, leases, fencing, clocks, ordering, and split-brain prevention.
Design sagas, deduplication, idempotency, and transaction boundaries across services.
Choose queue, pub/sub, log, workflow, batch, or stream abstractions from delivery and state requirements.
Define delivery semantics, ordering, partitioning, consumer state, replay, and idempotent processing.
Design retries, dead-letter handling, backpressure, buffering, and load shedding.
Design scheduled jobs, durable workflows, orchestration, choreography, and compensation.
Identify component, dependency, region, data, and operator failure modes and their blast radius.
Use timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, redundancy, overload controls, and graceful degradation appropriately.
Distinguish backup, replication, failover, and disaster recovery; derive RPO and RTO-driven strategies.
Test recovery, reconcile state after failover, and design for cascading dependency failure.
Design authentication, sessions, delegated authorization, resource ownership, and service identity.
Isolate tenants, secrets, keys, and sensitive data while controlling noisy neighbors and retention.
Protect APIs, webhooks, network edges, and resources from abuse, fraud, spam, DDoS, and unsafe consumption.
Model threats, auditability, privacy, non-repudiation, and secure defaults as architecture constraints.
Define useful telemetry, SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, and alerting tied to user impact.
Design health checks, deployment, feature flags, rollback, and compatible schema/API rollouts.
Design runbooks, escalation, incident response, and postmortem learning loops.
Reduce toil, simplify the system, and make operational responsibility explicit.
Analyze latency budgets, critical paths, queueing, contention, throughput, and saturation.
Choose vertical, horizontal, and autoscaling strategies and validate them with representative load tests.
Model unit economics, storage and transfer cost, and build-vs-buy or managed-vs-self-managed trade-offs.
Introduce complexity in stages and evolve architecture in response to measured constraints rather than forecasts alone.
